grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Plans: just the present
grammar[1].blocks[1].text: For a fixed plan Germans use the present: *Morgen gehe ich ins Kino.* werden is for promises, predictions and guesses.
grammar[1].fact: In German you rarely need the future tense for plans: *Morgen fahre ich nach Köln* is perfectly fine. Use *werden* to promise (*Ich werde dich anrufen*) or to guess (*Er wird wohl krank sein*). English speakers who say *werden* everywhere sound as if making vows.

document.intro: A real board at a fair, in chalk, one word per slat: the fish is cooked on an open fire right beside it. *Gegart* means cooked, *geräuchert* means smoked, *Buchenholz* is beech wood.
document.fact: German fairs are also food markets: *gebrannte Mandeln*, burnt almonds, are the smell of every one of them, and a *Lebkuchenherz*, a gingerbread heart on a ribbon, says something rude or romantic in icing.
reading.intro: Lena is thirty next week, so Maya has taken her to the fair in Stuttgart. In a small purple tent behind the Ferris wheel sits Madame Olga, and twenty euros later she has taken Lena’s hand and closed her eyes.
reading.fact: The Cannstatter Volksfest began in 1818, when the King of Württemberg wanted to cheer people up after a famine. It runs for about 17 days, with some 4 million visitors, and many Stuttgarters consider it superior to the Oktoberfest in every way that matters. Do not raise this in Munich.
